**Donald A. Yerxa** (born July 19, 1950) is an American author, editor, and historian.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Donald_A._Yerxa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Yerxa received his [bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History "History") from the [Eastern Nazarene College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Nazarene_College "Eastern Nazarene College") in 1972 and a [master's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master's_degree "Master's degree") (1974) and [Ph.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ph.D. "Ph.D.") (1982) from the [University of Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maine "University of Maine") on a university [fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow#Graduate_school_fellowships "Fellow"). He was a director of The Historical Society (THS)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-1) at [Boston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University "Boston University") and a senior editor of _[Historically Speaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically\_Speaking\_(journal) "Historically Speaking (journal)")_, published by the [Johns Hopkins University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University_Press "Johns Hopkins University Press").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-2)

Yerxa is the former chair of the History Department at his [alma mater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alma_mater "Alma mater"), the [Eastern Nazarene College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Nazarene_College "Eastern Nazarene College"), where he taught from 1977 to 2014,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-crusaders-3) and launched the history department's distinguished lecture series in the 1990s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-4) He was editor of the Conference on Faith and History's journal _[Fides et Historia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fides\_et\_Historia "Fides et Historia")_ from 2011 to 2020.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-5) He was a guest co-editor for the _European Review's_, forum on the [Scientific Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Revolution "Scientific Revolution"), and was a contributing editor for _[Books and Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Books\_&\_Culture "Books & Culture")_ magazine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-6) He was a frequent contributor to the _Research News & Opportunities in Science and Theology_ publication for the [John Templeton Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Templeton_Foundation "John Templeton Foundation") (JTF) and has been a multiple grant recipient.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-7)

## Published works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Donald_A._Yerxa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Published works")]

Yerxa has written scores of articles, review essays, book reviews, and encyclopedia entries for a number of publications. He has also conducted over one hundred published interviews of prominent historians and scholars from other disciplines. He is the author of three books, two on [naval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval "Naval") history: _Admirals and Empire,_[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-8) and _The Burning of Falmouth_,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-9) and _Species of Origins: America’s Search for a Creation Story_[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-10) with coauthor [Karl Giberson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Giberson "Karl Giberson"). _Admirals_ was described as "solidly researched, clearly and economically written, and intelligently conceived... a useful synthesis filling a gap in the existing literature,"[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-11)_Species of Origins_ was widely reviewed as a uniquely even-handed and concise contribution to the scholarship on the [creation–evolution controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creation%E2%80%93evolution_controversy "Creation–evolution controversy") in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). Galileo scholar William Shea lauded the account as the "best-written and most perceptive of the current accounts available,"[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-12) while author [Edward Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Larson "Edward Larson") described it as the "next best thing for those of us not enrolled in their courses."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-13) Professor of science [Michael Ruse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ruse "Michael Ruse") described it as “a simply invaluable primer on the subject that should be made compulsory reading for all who have ever thought on science-and-religion ... I can think of no better place to start into the debate about origins — creationism or evolution — than with this book.”[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-14) It has been the subject of and catalyst for various discussions, conferences, and other books.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-15)

Yerxa has also edited seven volumes in the _Historians in Conversation_ series for the [University of South Carolina Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_South_Carolina_Press "University of South Carolina Press"). And he has also two edited other volumes: _British Abolitionism, Moral Progress, and Big Questions in History_ (University of South Carolina Press, 2012) and _Religion and Innovation: Antagonists or Partners_ (Bloomsbury, 2016).

**Donald A. Yerxa** (born July 19, 1950) is an American author, editor, and historian.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Donald_A._Yerxa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Yerxa received his [bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History "History") from the [Eastern Nazarene College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Nazarene_College "Eastern Nazarene College") in 1972 and a [master's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master's_degree "Master's degree") (1974) and [Ph.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ph.D. "Ph.D.") (1982) from the [University of Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maine "University of Maine") on a university [fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow#Graduate_school_fellowships "Fellow"). He was a director of The Historical Society (THS)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-1) at [Boston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University "Boston University") and a senior editor of _[Historically Speaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically\_Speaking\_(journal) "Historically Speaking (journal)")_, published by the [Johns Hopkins University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University_Press "Johns Hopkins University Press").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-2)

Yerxa is the former chair of the History Department at his [alma mater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alma_mater "Alma mater"), the [Eastern Nazarene College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Nazarene_College "Eastern Nazarene College"), where he taught from 1977 to 2014,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-crusaders-3) and launched the history department's distinguished lecture series in the 1990s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-4) He was editor of the Conference on Faith and History's journal _[Fides et Historia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fides\_et\_Historia "Fides et Historia")_ from 2011 to 2020.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-5) He was a guest co-editor for the _European Review's_, forum on the [Scientific Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Revolution "Scientific Revolution"), and was a contributing editor for _[Books and Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Books\_&\_Culture "Books & Culture")_ magazine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-6) He was a frequent contributor to the _Research News & Opportunities in Science and Theology_ publication for the [John Templeton Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Templeton_Foundation "John Templeton Foundation") (JTF) and has been a multiple grant recipient.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-7)

## Published works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Donald_A._Yerxa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Published works")]

Yerxa has written scores of articles, review essays, book reviews, and encyclopedia entries for a number of publications. He has also conducted over one hundred published interviews of prominent historians and scholars from other disciplines. He is the author of three books, two on [naval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval "Naval") history: _Admirals and Empire,_[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-8) and _The Burning of Falmouth_,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-9) and _Species of Origins: America’s Search for a Creation Story_[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-10) with coauthor [Karl Giberson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Giberson "Karl Giberson"). _Admirals_ was described as "solidly researched, clearly and economically written, and intelligently conceived... a useful synthesis filling a gap in the existing literature,"[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-11)_Species of Origins_ was widely reviewed as a uniquely even-handed and concise contribution to the scholarship on the [creation–evolution controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creation%E2%80%93evolution_controversy "Creation–evolution controversy") in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). Galileo scholar William Shea lauded the account as the "best-written and most perceptive of the current accounts available,"[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-12) while author [Edward Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Larson "Edward Larson") described it as the "next best thing for those of us not enrolled in their courses."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-13) Professor of science [Michael Ruse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ruse "Michael Ruse") described it as “a simply invaluable primer on the subject that should be made compulsory reading for all who have ever thought on science-and-religion ... I can think of no better place to start into the debate about origins — creationism or evolution — than with this book.”[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-14) It has been the subject of and catalyst for various discussions, conferences, and other books.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-15)

Yerxa has also edited seven volumes in the _Historians in Conversation_ series for the [University of South Carolina Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_South_Carolina_Press "University of South Carolina Press"). And he has also two edited other volumes: _British Abolitionism, Moral Progress, and Big Questions in History_ (University of South Carolina Press, 2012) and _Religion and Innovation: Antagonists or Partners_ (Bloomsbury, 2016).

Yerxa is assistant director of the Historical Society ![Image 14](https://www.bu.edu/historic/london/yerxa.jpg)and editor of its bulletin, _Historically Speaking_. He is also professor of history at Eastern Nazarene College. He was trained as a naval historian, receiving his M.A. and Ph.D. from the University of Maine, where he studied under two of the leading naval historians of the 20th century, Robert Greenlaugh Albion and Clark Reynolds. He has written two books: _The Burning of Falmouth, 1775_ (Maine Historical Society, 1975) and _Admirals and Empire: The United States Navy and the Caribbean, 1898-1945_ (University of South Carolina Press, 1991). He has also done work in the history of science and religion, co-authoring _Species of Origins: America’s Search for a Creation Story_ (Rowman & Littlefield, 2002). He is co-editor of a new University of South Carolina Press book series, _Historians in Conversation: Understanding the Past_. Yerxa is a contributing editor of _Books & Culture_ and serves on the editorial board of _New Global Studies_. He is a resident member of the Colonial Society of Massachusetts. His articles and interviews have appeared in a wide variety of publications including _Military Affairs_, the _Naval War College Review_, _Mariner’s Mirror_, _Fides et Historia_, _Books & Culture_, _Science & Spirit_, and _Historically Speaking_. A generation ago, intellectual history was in crisis. Today there is evidence everywhere that intellectual history speaks to the dominant historiography of our day; its insights and methods have become part of the common coin of the most significant work currently being done. And yet there is a lingering sense that intellectual history as intellectual history is a field safely ignored by most historians, that the old arguments for its dismissal still retain life, that intellectual historians sit on the margin of the history department where more mainstream historians are free to characterize them as not quite historians. Not long after that, it will appear on [Project Muse](http://muse.jhu.edu/journals/historically_speaking/). The September issue includes a variety of essays, interviews, and an extended forum on the current state of intellectual history. Senior editor Donald Yerxa [![Image 2](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEidA_6MNZ-573CohoRdE7aZPfDYPpcuDpzEGbbRwI6HyvG5Hn_m0DwH9LbMJvJEtDOF3uiR5dogEpi5uNWGOskVM3TIxHlPtHtVbEgKyseZUDSMcQhzSdaY3QJzUhndx71pRLMxl4tvc0eD/s400/sept_09_hs.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEidA_6MNZ-573CohoRdE7aZPfDYPpcuDpzEGbbRwI6HyvG5Hn_m0DwH9LbMJvJEtDOF3uiR5dogEpi5uNWGOskVM3TIxHlPtHtVbEgKyseZUDSMcQhzSdaY3QJzUhndx71pRLMxl4tvc0eD/s1600-h/sept_09_hs.jpg)introduces the forum as follows: The sense that the discipline of history was marginalizing traditional fields like diplomatic, economic, military, constitutional, and intellectual history—fields that critics charge focus far too much on elite decision makers—was a major concern of the founders of the Historical Society. As the Society enters its second decade, it is appropriate to revisit this matter, especially when the status of traditional historical fields is still debated, most recently in the pages of the New York Times (Patricia Cohen, [“Great Caesar’s Ghost! Are Traditional History Courses Vanishing?”](http://www.nytimes.com/2009/06/11/books/11hist.html) June 10, 2009). [[See this earlier post on the matter here](http://histsociety.blogspot.com/2009/06/which-history.html).] Historically Speaking has received a generous grant from the Earhart Foundation to publish a series of forums examining the state of four traditional fields that some believe are being neglected in today’s academy. Intellectual history is the focus of our first forum. We asked [Daniel Wickberg](http://www.utdallas.edu/ah/people/faculty_detail.php?faculty_id=1261), a cogent observer of historiographical trends, to write the lead essay. Three distinguished intellectual historians—[David Hollinger](http://history.berkeley.edu/faculty/Hollinger/), [Sarah Igo](http://www.vanderbilt.edu/historydept/igo.html), and [Wilfred McClay](http://www.utc.edu/Research/SunTrustChair/chair_mcclay_index.html)—respond, followed by Wickberg’s rejoinder. In his lead essay, Daniel Wickberg writes: What the transformations wrought by both the linguistic and cultural turns point to is just how much the methods, approaches, and theoretical concerns that have characterized intellectual history have become central to mainstream historical practice. A generation ago, intellectual history was in crisis. Today there is evidence everywhere that intellectual history speaks to the dominant historiography of our day; its insights and methods have become part of the common coin of the most significant work currently being done. And yet there is a lingering sense that intellectual history as intellectual history is a field safely ignored by most historians, that the old arguments for its dismissal still retain life, that intellectual historians sit on the margin of the history department where more mainstream historians are free to characterize them as not quite historians. So the contemporary condition of intellectual history is somewhat paradoxical. He advocates for a reevaluation of the concept of civilization, stressing the need to recognize the similarities and shared developments between ancient societies and contemporary ones.

This volume presents a series of studies by scholars working in Middle Eastern archaeology who actively apply social theory to interpret their fieldwork. It highlights the value of using social theory in the interpretation of fieldwork in a region where, traditionally, such approaches have not played a major role. There are a number of factors that account for why social theory is often under-exploited by archaeologists in this part of the world. In many countries, where large numbers of the foreign archaeologists are involved, a division between those doing fieldwork and those undertaking archaeological interpretation can easily arise. Or, the lack of interest in social theory may stem from a legacy of positivism that overrides other approaches. There is also the fact that archaeology and anthropology often belong to separate academic departments and are considered to be two separate and disconnected disciplines. In some cases, the centrality of historical paradigms has precluded the use of social theory. There are also divisions between universities and other research institutions, such as departments of antiquities, which is not conductive to interdisciplinary cooperation. This factor is especially debilitating in contexts of rapid destruction of sites and the exponential growth of salvage excavations and emergency surveys. The papers presented here integrate a range of perspectives including 'New' or 'Processual' archaeology, Marxist, 'Post-Processual', evolutionist, cognitive, symbolic, and Cyber archaeologies, and touch on many topics including 3D representation, GIS, mapping and social theory, semiotics and linguistics, gender and bioarchaeology, social and technical identities, and modern historical modelling and social practices in Middle Eastern archaeology.

![Image 14: sparkles](https://c.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

What key findings challenge existing notions of civilization in the ancient Near East?add

Recent research shows extensive cultural exchanges across the Near East long before writing systems existed, altering perspectives on civilization. For instance, material flows like metals and oils reveal interconnectivity across regions such as Turkmenistan and Arabia.

How have archaeological discoveries reshaped the understanding of ancient trade relationships?add

Evidence suggests that trade in everyday items, alongside luxury goods, highlights a complex network in ancient societies. These findings, accumulating continuously, underscore the interconnectedness of regions from the Indus Valley to the Mediterranean.

What implications do new findings have for the concept of civilization?add

The idea of civilization may oversimplify historical connections and shared practices among societies. Wengrow argues that understanding these connections challenges the linear progression narrative often associated with civilization.

How does the interplay of commerce and cosmology manifest in ancient societies?add

Elites in ancient Mesopotamia intertwined commerce with religious beliefs, showcasing how trade was regulated through divine concepts. This relationship echoes modern economic systems, where branding parallels sacred rituals.

Why has the significance of the ancient Near East been overlooked in grand narratives?add

Grand historical accounts often neglect the ancient Near East due to biases towards localized perspectives. Scholars like Daniel Lord Smail emphasize a unified human history, yet fail to recognize important transitional dynamics in these ancient societies.

Anthropology of the Middle East has implicitly and explicitly been a journal with a regional orientation. Most previous issues, however, have added a thematic dimension to this regional orientation, and the same applies to this special issue. The chosen theme is anthropological archaeology, given the fact that this school in archaeology has been responsible for tremendous progress in Middle Eastern archaeology and has advanced our knowledge of the ancient Middle East by leaps and bounds. Anthropological archaeology has been a major player in Middle Eastern archaeology for the past half-century, and no other school in Middle Eastern archaeology can claim to have been immune from its influence, whether in matters of theory or, more visibly, in methodology. Archaeology of the Middle East (Near East, in archaeological parlance) always has been an enticing field for professional archaeologists and archaeology aficionados alike. Beginning in the mid-nineteenth century and continuing into the early decades of the twentieth century, large-scale and high-profile excavations, predominantly inspired by biblical accounts or imperial competition among European powers, marked the 'Golden Age' of archaeology in the Middle East, when many excavated archaeological sites revealed awe-inspiring palaces of long-forgotten rulers and temples of heathen gods and, in the absence of any meaningful set of antiquities laws, poured invaluable artefacts and hoards of cuneiform tablets into major museums in Europe and the United States. Following World War II, as the new economic conditions in the West hindered such grandiose archaeological adventures, another, more subtle movement in archaeology was about to shift the focus from large-scale excavations aimed, among other things, at discovering lost cities and civilisations to much smaller exposures focused on more humble, but arguably more important, questions pertaining to the early stages of human development. The rise of New Archaeology in the United States and England was changing the theoretical and methodological configuration of archaeology and pushing for a closer intellectual and methodological affiliation with anthropology and other social and natural sciences.

[Ianir Milevski](https://conicet.academia.edu/IanirMilevski), [Thomas E Levy](https://ucsd.academia.edu/TomLevy)

This volume presents a series of studies by scholars working in Middle Eastern archaeology who actively apply social theory to interpret their fieldwork. It highlights the value of using social theory in the interpretation of fieldwork in a region where, traditionally, such approaches have not played a major role. There are a number of factors that account for why social theory is often under-exploited by archaeologists in this part of the world. In many countries, where large numbers of the foreign archaeologists are involved, a division between those doing fieldwork and those undertaking archaeological interpretation can easily arise. Or, the lack of interest in social theory may stem from a legacy of positivism that overrides other approaches. There is also the fact that archaeology and anthropology often belong to separate academic departments and are considered to be two separate and disconnected disciplines. In some cases, the centrality of historical paradigms has precluded the use of social theory. There are also divisions between universities and other research institutions, such as departments of antiquities, which is not conductive to interdisciplinary cooperation. This factor is especially debilitating in contexts of rapid destruction of sites and the exponential growth of salvage excavations and emergency surveys. The papers presented here integrate a range of perspectives including 'New' or 'Processual' archaeology, Marxist, 'Post-Processual', evolutionist, cognitive, symbolic, and Cyber archaeologies, and touch on many topics including 3D representation, GIS, mapping and social theory, semiotics and linguistics, gender and bioarchaeology, social and technical identities, and modern historical modelling and social practices in Middle Eastern archaeology.

This tension between center and periphery has always been a source of interest and inspiration in the history of Sijilmasa and for precisely this reason, a study incorporating the historical and archaeological data in an illustration of this dynamic at the site-wide scale would be an essential resource. Anthropology of the Middle East has implicitly and explicitly been a journal with a regional orientation. Most previous issues, however, have added a thematic dimension to this regional orientation, and the same applies to this special issue. The chosen theme is anthropological archaeology, given the fact that this school in archaeology has been responsible for tremendous progress in Middle Eastern archaeology and has advanced our knowledge of the ancient Middle East by leaps and bounds. Anthropological archaeology has been a major player in Middle Eastern archaeology for the past half-century, and no other school in Middle Eastern archaeology can claim to have been immune from its influence, whether in matters of theory or, more visibly, in methodology. Archaeology of the Middle East (Near East, in archaeological parlance) always has been an enticing field for professional archaeologists and archaeology aficionados alike. Beginning in the mid-nineteenth century and continuing into the early decades of the twentieth century, large-scale and high-profile excavations, predominantly inspired by biblical accounts or imperial competition among European powers, marked the 'Golden Age' of archaeology in the Middle East, when many excavated archaeological sites revealed awe-inspiring palaces of long-forgotten rulers and temples of heathen gods and, in the absence of any meaningful set of antiquities laws, poured invaluable artefacts and hoards of cuneiform tablets into major museums in Europe and the United States. Following World War II, as the new economic conditions in the West hindered such grandiose archaeological adventures, another, more subtle movement in archaeology was about to shift the focus from large-scale excavations aimed, among other things, at discovering lost cities and civilisations to much smaller exposures focused on more humble, but arguably more important, questions pertaining to the early stages of human development. The rise of New Archaeology in the United States and England was changing the theoretical and methodological configuration of archaeology and pushing for a closer intellectual and methodological affiliation with anthropology and other social and natural sciences.

The project aims to conduct fieldwork at Tepe Qaleh Naneh, an archaeological site located in the Marivan area in northern central Zagros, Iran. The excavations have provided valuable insights into the occupational deposits at the site, revealing burials, wall structures, and various materials such as pottery and lithics. These deposits span from the Chalcolithic to Islamic periods, with a particular focus on the Late Chalcolithic period, which appears to be the most significant occupation phase. Laboratory analyses have been conducted on organic samples, including charcoals and bones, as well as on items such as obsidian objects. These analyses have enabled the study of adaptation models and developmental patterns in a region, the northern central Zagros, which remains relatively understudied. The ecosystem of Tepeh Qaleh Naneh and Marivan plain, between the Middle Chalcolithic period to Bronze age, consists of extensive vegetation of oak forest-steppe And the amount of precipitation, at least in the Late Chalcolithic period, was not less than 600 mm. the material culture discovered at Tepe Qaleh Naneh indicates an increase in social complexity, as evidenced by the presence of stone mace-heads (ceremonial tools), specialized productions such as painted pottery, and evidence of long-distance contacts. Interestingly, the site appears to have stronger connections with Mesopotamia than with western Iran. The identification of Uruk pottery, including beveled-rim bowls, suggests commercial and cultural relations between the society in the Marivan region and northern Mesopotamia during the late Chalcolithic period. These findings shed light on the gradual differentiation of society during the Chalcolithic period, a critical period that witnessed the emergence of the first porto-urban communities in southern Mesopotamia. Even if the Zagros communities followed a similar trend during the Chalcolithic period, they also developed local traditions as response to interregional contacts.

Original discussions on the public role of history and historians from a pantheon of notable experts  
  
Recent Themes on Historians and the Public represents some of the best recent writing on the public role of historians. These articles and interviews from Historically Speaking examine the relationship between historians and their audiences. Award-winning "popular historian" Adam Hochschild begins by discussing the relationship between popular and academic history. An all-star cast of historians and editors offer their responses, forming a fascinating extended conversation. This forum addresses questions such as what the public role of the historian should be and whether practicing history requires a license. In addition the book contains a candid exchange about the state of the history profession at the beginning of the twenty-first century.   
  
Designed to engage both students and general readers, Recent Themes on Historians and the Public illuminates the controversy over the role of historians in the public sphere.

### About the Author

Donald Yerxa was born in Portland, Maine in 1950. From 2001 until 2013, he was a senior editor of Historically Speaking, a journal of historical ideas published by The Johns Hopkins University Press, and from 2011 to 2020, he was editor of Fides et Historia, the peer-reviewed journal of the Conference on Faith and History. He served as an officer of the Historical Society from 2001 to 2014. He is professor of history emeritus at Eastern Nazarene College in Quincy, MA and now resides in Florida.

Original discussions on the public role of history and historians from a pantheon of notable experts  
  
Recent Themes on Historians and the Public represents some of the best recent writing on the public role of historians. These articles and interviews from Historically Speaking examine the relationship between historians and their audiences. Award-winning "popular historian" Adam Hochschild begins by discussing the relationship between popular and academic history. An all-star cast of historians and editors offer their responses, forming a fascinating extended conversation. This forum addresses questions such as what the public role of the historian should be and whether practicing history requires a license. In addition the book contains a candid exchange about the state of the history profession at the beginning of the twenty-first century.

Donald Yerxa was born in Portland, Maine in 1950. From 2001 until 2013, he was a senior editor of Historically Speaking, a journal of historical ideas published by The Johns Hopkins University Press, and from 2011 to 2020, he was editor of Fides et Historia, the peer-reviewed journal of the Conference on Faith and History. He served as an officer of the Historical Society from 2001 to 2014. He is professor of history emeritus at Eastern Nazarene College in Quincy, MA and now resides in Florida.

Not long after that, it will appear on [Project Muse](http://muse.jhu.edu/journals/historically_speaking/). The September issue includes a variety of essays, interviews, and an extended forum on the current state of intellectual history. Senior editor Donald Yerxa [![Image 2](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEidA_6MNZ-573CohoRdE7aZPfDYPpcuDpzEGbbRwI6HyvG5Hn_m0DwH9LbMJvJEtDOF3uiR5dogEpi5uNWGOskVM3TIxHlPtHtVbEgKyseZUDSMcQhzSdaY3QJzUhndx71pRLMxl4tvc0eD/s400/sept_09_hs.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEidA_6MNZ-573CohoRdE7aZPfDYPpcuDpzEGbbRwI6HyvG5Hn_m0DwH9LbMJvJEtDOF3uiR5dogEpi5uNWGOskVM3TIxHlPtHtVbEgKyseZUDSMcQhzSdaY3QJzUhndx71pRLMxl4tvc0eD/s1600-h/sept_09_hs.jpg)introduces the forum as follows: The sense that the discipline of history was marginalizing traditional fields like diplomatic, economic, military, constitutional, and intellectual history—fields that critics charge focus far too much on elite decision makers—was a major concern of the founders of the Historical Society. As the Society enters its second decade, it is appropriate to revisit this matter, especially when the status of traditional historical fields is still debated, most recently in the pages of the New York Times (Patricia Cohen, [“Great Caesar’s Ghost! Are Traditional History Courses Vanishing?”](http://www.nytimes.com/2009/06/11/books/11hist.html) June 10, 2009). [[See this earlier post on the matter here](http://histsociety.blogspot.com/2009/06/which-history.html).] Historically Speaking has received a generous grant from the Earhart Foundation to publish a series of forums examining the state of four traditional fields that some believe are being neglected in today’s academy. Intellectual history is the focus of our first forum. We asked [Daniel Wickberg](http://www.utdallas.edu/ah/people/faculty_detail.php?faculty_id=1261), a cogent observer of historiographical trends, to write the lead essay. Three distinguished intellectual historians—[David Hollinger](http://history.berkeley.edu/faculty/Hollinger/), [Sarah Igo](http://www.vanderbilt.edu/historydept/igo.html), and [Wilfred McClay](http://www.utc.edu/Research/SunTrustChair/chair_mcclay_index.html)—respond, followed by Wickberg’s rejoinder. In his lead essay, Daniel Wickberg writes: What the transformations wrought by both the linguistic and cultural turns point to is just how much the methods, approaches, and theoretical concerns that have characterized intellectual history have become central to mainstream historical practice. A generation ago, intellectual history was in crisis. Today there is evidence everywhere that intellectual history speaks to the dominant historiography of our day; its insights and methods have become part of the common coin of the most significant work currently being done. And yet there is a lingering sense that intellectual history as intellectual history is a field safely ignored by most historians, that the old arguments for its dismissal still retain life, that intellectual historians sit on the margin of the history department where more mainstream historians are free to characterize them as not quite historians. So the contemporary condition of intellectual history is somewhat paradoxical. Not long after that, it will appear on [Project Muse](http://muse.jhu.edu/journals/historically_speaking/). The September issue includes a variety of essays, interviews, and an extended forum on the current state of intellectual history. Senior editor Donald Yerxa [![Image 2](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEidA_6MNZ-573CohoRdE7aZPfDYPpcuDpzEGbbRwI6HyvG5Hn_m0DwH9LbMJvJEtDOF3uiR5dogEpi5uNWGOskVM3TIxHlPtHtVbEgKyseZUDSMcQhzSdaY3QJzUhndx71pRLMxl4tvc0eD/s400/sept_09_hs.jpg)](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEidA_6MNZ-573CohoRdE7aZPfDYPpcuDpzEGbbRwI6HyvG5Hn_m0DwH9LbMJvJEtDOF3uiR5dogEpi5uNWGOskVM3TIxHlPtHtVbEgKyseZUDSMcQhzSdaY3QJzUhndx71pRLMxl4tvc0eD/s1600-h/sept_09_hs.jpg)introduces the forum as follows: The sense that the discipline of history was marginalizing traditional fields like diplomatic, economic, military, constitutional, and intellectual history—fields that critics charge focus far too much on elite decision makers—was a major concern of the founders of the Historical Society. As the Society enters its second decade, it is appropriate to revisit this matter, especially when the status of traditional historical fields is still debated, most recently in the pages of the New York Times (Patricia Cohen, [“Great Caesar’s Ghost! Are Traditional History Courses Vanishing?”](http://www.nytimes.com/2009/06/11/books/11hist.html) June 10, 2009). [[See this earlier post on the matter here](http://histsociety.blogspot.com/2009/06/which-history.html).] Historically Speaking has received a generous grant from the Earhart Foundation to publish a series of forums examining the state of four traditional fields that some believe are being neglected in today’s academy. Intellectual history is the focus of our first forum. We asked [Daniel Wickberg](http://www.utdallas.edu/ah/people/faculty_detail.php?faculty_id=1261), a cogent observer of historiographical trends, to write the lead essay. Three distinguished intellectual historians—[David Hollinger](http://history.berkeley.edu/faculty/Hollinger/), [Sarah Igo](http://www.vanderbilt.edu/historydept/igo.html), and [Wilfred McClay](http://www.utc.edu/Research/SunTrustChair/chair_mcclay_index.html)—respond, followed by Wickberg’s rejoinder. In his lead essay, Daniel Wickberg writes: What the transformations wrought by both the linguistic and cultural turns point to is just how much the methods, approaches, and theoretical concerns that have characterized intellectual history have become central to mainstream historical practice. A generation ago, intellectual history was in crisis. Today there is evidence everywhere that intellectual history speaks to the dominant historiography of our day; its insights and methods have become part of the common coin of the most significant work currently being done. And yet there is a lingering sense that intellectual history as intellectual history is a field safely ignored by most historians, that the old arguments for its dismissal still retain life, that intellectual historians sit on the margin of the history department where more mainstream historians are free to characterize them as not quite historians. So the contemporary condition of intellectual history is somewhat paradoxical. ## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Donald_A._Yerxa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Yerxa received his [bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History "History") from the [Eastern Nazarene College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Nazarene_College "Eastern Nazarene College") in 1972 and a [master's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master's_degree "Master's degree") (1974) and [Ph.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ph.D. "Ph.D.") (1982) from the [University of Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maine "University of Maine") on a university [fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow#Graduate_school_fellowships "Fellow"). He was a director of The Historical Society (THS)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-1) at [Boston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University "Boston University") and a senior editor of _[Historically Speaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically\_Speaking\_(journal) "Historically Speaking (journal)")_, published by the [Johns Hopkins University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University_Press "Johns Hopkins University Press").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-2)

Yerxa is the former chair of the History Department at his [alma mater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alma_mater "Alma mater"), the [Eastern Nazarene College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Nazarene_College "Eastern Nazarene College"), where he taught from 1977 to 2014,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-crusaders-3) and launched the history department's distinguished lecture series in the 1990s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-4) He was editor of the Conference on Faith and History's journal _[Fides et Historia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fides\_et\_Historia "Fides et Historia")_ from 2011 to 2020.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-5) He was a guest co-editor for the _European Review's_, forum on the [Scientific Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Revolution "Scientific Revolution"), and was a contributing editor for _[Books and Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Books\_&\_Culture "Books & Culture")_ magazine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-6) He was a frequent contributor to the _Research News & Opportunities in Science and Theology_ publication for the [John Templeton Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Templeton_Foundation "John Templeton Foundation") (JTF) and has been a multiple grant recipient.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-7)

## Published works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Donald_A._Yerxa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Published works")]

Yerxa has written scores of articles, review essays, book reviews, and encyclopedia entries for a number of publications. He has also conducted over one hundred published interviews of prominent historians and scholars from other disciplines. He is the author of three books, two on [naval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval "Naval") history: _Admirals and Empire,_[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-8) and _The Burning of Falmouth_,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-9) and _Species of Origins: America’s Search for a Creation Story_[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-10) with coauthor [Karl Giberson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Giberson "Karl Giberson"). _Admirals_ was described as "solidly researched, clearly and economically written, and intelligently conceived... a useful synthesis filling a gap in the existing literature,"[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-11)_Species of Origins_ was widely reviewed as a uniquely even-handed and concise contribution to the scholarship on the [creation–evolution controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creation%E2%80%93evolution_controversy "Creation–evolution controversy") in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). Galileo scholar William Shea lauded the account as the "best-written and most perceptive of the current accounts available,"[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-12) while author [Edward Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Larson "Edward Larson") described it as the "next best thing for those of us not enrolled in their courses."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-13) Professor of science [Michael Ruse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ruse "Michael Ruse") described it as “a simply invaluable primer on the subject that should be made compulsory reading for all who have ever thought on science-and-religion ... I can think of no better place to start into the debate about origins — creationism or evolution — than with this book.”[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-14) It has been the subject of and catalyst for various discussions, conferences, and other books.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-15)

Yerxa has also edited seven volumes in the _Historians in Conversation_ series for the [University of South Carolina Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_South_Carolina_Press "University of South Carolina Press"). And he has also two edited other volumes: _British Abolitionism, Moral Progress, and Big Questions in History_ (University of South Carolina Press, 2012) and _Religion and Innovation: Antagonists or Partners_ (Bloomsbury, 2016).

**Donald A. Yerxa** (born July 19, 1950) is an American author, editor, and historian.

## Biography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Donald_A._Yerxa&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Yerxa received his [bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History "History") from the [Eastern Nazarene College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Nazarene_College "Eastern Nazarene College") in 1972 and a [master's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master's_degree "Master's degree") (1974) and [Ph.D.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ph.D. "Ph.D.") (1982) from the [University of Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maine "University of Maine") on a university [fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fellow#Graduate_school_fellowships "Fellow"). He was a director of The Historical Society (THS)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-1) at [Boston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University "Boston University") and a senior editor of _[Historically Speaking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historically\_Speaking\_(journal) "Historically Speaking (journal)")_, published by the [Johns Hopkins University Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johns_Hopkins_University_Press "Johns Hopkins University Press").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-2)

Yerxa is the former chair of the History Department at his [alma mater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alma_mater "Alma mater"), the [Eastern Nazarene College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Nazarene_College "Eastern Nazarene College"), where he taught from 1977 to 2014,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-crusaders-3) and launched the history department's distinguished lecture series in the 1990s.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-4) He was editor of the Conference on Faith and History's journal _[Fides et Historia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fides\_et\_Historia "Fides et Historia")_ from 2011 to 2020.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-5) He was a guest co-editor for the _European Review's_, forum on the [Scientific Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Revolution "Scientific Revolution"), and was a contributing editor for _[Books and Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Books\_&\_Culture "Books & Culture")_ magazine.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-6) He was a frequent contributor to the _Research News & Opportunities in Science and Theology_ publication for the [John Templeton Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Templeton_Foundation "John Templeton Foundation") (JTF) and has been a multiple grant recipient.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-7)

## Published works

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Donald_A._Yerxa&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Published works")]

Yerxa has written scores of articles, review essays, book reviews, and encyclopedia entries for a number of publications. He has also conducted over one hundred published interviews of prominent historians and scholars from other disciplines. He is the author of three books, two on [naval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naval "Naval") history: _Admirals and Empire,_[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-8) and _The Burning of Falmouth_,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-9) and _Species of Origins: America’s Search for a Creation Story_[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-10) with coauthor [Karl Giberson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Giberson "Karl Giberson"). _Admirals_ was described as "solidly researched, clearly and economically written, and intelligently conceived... a useful synthesis filling a gap in the existing literature,"[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-11)_Species of Origins_ was widely reviewed as a uniquely even-handed and concise contribution to the scholarship on the [creation–evolution controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creation%E2%80%93evolution_controversy "Creation–evolution controversy") in the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"). Galileo scholar William Shea lauded the account as the "best-written and most perceptive of the current accounts available,"[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-12) while author [Edward Larson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Larson "Edward Larson") described it as the "next best thing for those of us not enrolled in their courses."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-13) Professor of science [Michael Ruse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Ruse "Michael Ruse") described it as “a simply invaluable primer on the subject that should be made compulsory reading for all who have ever thought on science-and-religion ... I can think of no better place to start into the debate about origins — creationism or evolution — than with this book.”[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-14) It has been the subject of and catalyst for various discussions, conferences, and other books.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_A._Yerxa#cite_note-15)

Yerxa has also edited seven volumes in the _Historians in Conversation_ series for the [University of South Carolina Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_South_Carolina_Press "University of South Carolina Press"). And he has also two edited other volumes: _British Abolitionism, Moral Progress, and Big Questions in History_ (University of South Carolina Press, 2012) and _Religion and Innovation: Antagonists or Partners_ (Bloomsbury, 2016).

Described as "the New York Review of Books for history," Historically Speaking has emerged as one of the most distinctive historical publications in recent years, actively seeking out contributions from a pantheon of leading voices in historical discourse from both inside and outside academia. Recent Themes in World History and the History of the West represents some of the best writing on Western civilization and world history in the past five years.   
  
This collection of essays and interviews from Historically Speaking gives leading historians' approaches to the continually evolving field of world history, with a specific emphasis on the relationship of Western civilization to the history of the world. The book also discusses the effect of empire on global history and the many ways empire continues to manifest in the contemporary world. The contributors discuss world history as an intricate story of the connections within the global community, rather than a tidy, static narrative that attempts to summarize everything in our global past. In this volume the study of world history is presented as a constantly comparative endeavor, concerned with the major themes that link and divide humanity.

Donald Yerxa was born in Portland, Maine in 1950. From 2001 until 2013, he was a senior editor of Historically Speaking, a journal of historical ideas published by The Johns Hopkins University Press, and from 2011 to 2020, he was editor of Fides et Historia, the peer-reviewed journal of the Conference on Faith and History. He served as an officer of the Historical Society from 2001 to 2014. He is professor of history emeritus at Eastern Nazarene College in Quincy, MA and now resides in Florida.

New insights on global histories and Western civilization from leading scholars in the field  
  
Described as "the New York Review of Books for history," Historically Speaking has emerged as one of the most distinctive historical publications in recent years, actively seeking out contributions from a pantheon of leading voices in historical discourse from both inside and outside academia. Recent Themes in World History and the History of the West represents some of the best writing on Western civilization and world history in the past five years.   
  
This collection of essays and interviews from Historically Speaking gives leading historians' approaches to the continually evolving field of world history, with a specific emphasis on the relationship of Western civilization to the history of the world. The book also discusses the effect of empire on global history and the many ways empire continues to manifest in the contemporary world. The contributors discuss world history as an intricate story of the connections within the global community, rather than a tidy, static narrative that attempts to summarize everything in our global past. In this volume the study of world history is presented as a constantly comparative endeavor, concerned with the major themes that link and divide humanity.

March 13, 2026 Bourgeois 1 

John Lukacs (1924-2019) is best remembered for his histories of modern Europe, America, and the Second World War, as well as his philosophy of history. After his death, a variety of obituaries recounted his contributions on these topics. 1 Outside of obituaries, several historians have explored his writing in both Hungarian and English. 2 However, remembering him as nothing more than a historian of modern civilization may obscure his lengthy meditations on the novel. Lukacs the historian cannot be understood without his love of novels. Few have studied his extensive meditations on literature. Lee Congdon’s article “ The Reactionary 

Loyalties of John Lukacs” (2003) and Gé za Jeszensky’s “Civis Hungaricus : For Our Mistakes, Now We Alone Are Responsible ” (2023) mention Lukacs’s fascination but do little more. 3 The Hungarian historian voraciously read novels, and this obsession shaped his view of the historical craft. He most clearly articulated his indebtedness to the novel in his 1968 Historical Consciousness (1967) .4 In the 1985 republication, he lamented that “ Historical Consciousness 

was my least successful book; it received no notice at all in the very professional historical

For Lukacs, the reading of novels was more than a pastime. Novels instrumentally formed the way he thought. This obsession with novels began before he devoted his career to history. In his autobiography, 

Confessions of an Original Sinner (1991) , he remembered, “Around the age of thirteen I became 

an avid reader of novels – of all kinds of novels, not only historical ones; in fact, I was not

thing he “relished in certain novels was every kind of historical detail.” 7

Lukacs found these details in a variety of novels from across Europe and America. He admired F. Scott Fitzgerald as much as he did Charles Dickens. He read and reread the novels of Anthony Trollope into old age. 8 He recalled that in his teenage years, he “discovered the delights

While Lukacs believed that every novel is historical, he also cautioned that some historical novels convey false realities. However, his focus remained on those novelists who formed his own historical thinking. For decades, he turned to these writers to demonstrate the historicity of the novel.

In Historical Consciousness , Lukacs claimed that “In the broad sense, every novel is a historical novel .” 15  This definition does not adhere to a set of arbitrarily chosen rules. For a novel to be considered historical, it does not need to take place years before the author ’s life . It does not always recount the political and social events of a time, nor recreate the lives of certain historical personages. Lukacs’s dictum is not an attempt to define the sub-genre. To Lukacs, any novel that described real places, circumstances, and people could be considered historical. He saw the novel as an intrinsically historical genre. Very early in his career, Lukacs went so far as to predict the end of the novel and its absorption into historical writing. 16  He saw in many twentieth-century novelists an effort to write history with the form of a novel, rather than write a novel with the help of history. The French Jean Dutourd, American E.L. Doctorow, Russian Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, and many more wrote novels for the primary purpose of preserving history. Bibliographical Essay 

This thesis began as an inquiry into José Ortega y Gasset’s Meditations on Quixote. I

intended to study Ortega’s view of the novel and how it influenced John Lukacs. As the project 

evolved, the focus shifted to Lukacs. However, Ortega remained an instrumental figure to the project insofar as he influenced Lukacs. However, Lukacs became the main study of the project very early. The historiography of Lukacs ’s work is currently sparse. His students (John Rossi and John Rodden) have written multiple articles about him. 88  Other Historians, such as Richard Gamble, Lee Congdon, and John H. Ferrell have also written clearly about Lukacs’s legacy. 

Some Hungarian writers wrote about him. Among others, the historian and diplomat Géza Jeszensky, a friend of Lukacs, crafted an essay in memory of him. Many mentioned his love of novels, but few went further. Lukacs’s reflections on the novel are intrinsically woven into many 

of his other themes, such as the democratic age, historical consciousness, and others. For someone to fully understand the novel’s significance, he must be acquainted with these themes. 

In 2025, I worked with the John Lukacs papers at Notre Dame. Until 2019, no scholar had access to these papers. Even now, only a small group has worked with them. Gamble is the only historian who has both written about Lukacs and studied his archives. Letters to and from novelists, lecture notes, and unpublished drafts added greatly to this project. It became even clearer in the archives that Lukacs’s reflections on the novel went deeper permeated more than 

just his writing. Many materials have not been explored that may add to this discussion. For example, later in life, Lukacs began and continued an extensive correspondence with the

John Lukacs (1924-2019) is best remembered for his histories of modern Europe, America, and the Second World War, as well as his philosophy of history. After his death, a variety of obituaries recounted his contributions on these topics. 1 Outside of obituaries, several historians have explored his writing in both Hungarian and English. 2 However, remembering him as nothing more than a historian of modern civilization may obscure his lengthy meditations on the novel. Lukacs the historian cannot be understood without his love of novels. Few have studied his extensive meditations on literature. Lee Congdon’s article “ The Reactionary 

Loyalties of John Lukacs” (2003) and Gé za Jeszensky’s “Civis Hungaricus : For Our Mistakes, Now We Alone Are Responsible ” (2023) mention Lukacs’s fascination but do little more. 3 The Hungarian historian voraciously read novels, and this obsession shaped his view of the historical craft. He most clearly articulated his indebtedness to the novel in his 1968 Historical Consciousness (1967) .4 In the 1985 republication, he lamented that “ Historical Consciousness

In Historical Consciousness , Lukacs claimed that “In the broad sense, every novel is a historical novel .” 15  This definition does not adhere to a set of arbitrarily chosen rules. For a novel to be considered historical, it does not need to take place years before the author ’s life . It does not always recount the political and social events of a time, nor recreate the lives of certain historical personages. Lukacs’s dictum is not an attempt to define the sub-genre. To Lukacs, any novel that described real places, circumstances, and people could be considered historical. He saw the novel as an intrinsically historical genre. Very early in his career, Lukacs went so far as to predict the end of the novel and its absorption into historical writing. 16  He saw in many twentieth-century novelists an effort to write history with the form of a novel, rather than write a novel with the help of history. The French Jean Dutourd, American E.L. Doctorow, Russian Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, and many more wrote novels for the primary purpose of preserving history. More forebodingly, in his 1981 essay “Doctorow urlitzer or History in Ragtime ,” Lukacs predicted the end of serious literature in the West. Despite this later pessimism, Lukacs allowed the novel to greatly influence his writing and teaching styles. His student John Rossi

The same historical limitations apply to the mythical and fantastical novels, which began appearing before modern realistic literature. They differ from the epic in that they do return to a reachable past. They do recreate the world as it was at some point in history. However, their fantastical elements blur the lines between myth and reality. Later in Meditations on Quixote, 

Ortega described mythical and chivalric literature as a kind of bridge between the epic and the novel: 

The Greek novel is only corrupted history, divinely corrupted by the myth, or rather, like the voyage to the country of the Arimaspi, fantastic geography, memories of voyages which the myth has distorted and later put together again freely. To the same genre belongs all literature of imagination, all that is called story, ballad, legend, and books of chivalry. They always deal with some historical material which the myth has distorted and reabsorbed. 46 

Ortega acknowledged that these myths contain historical elements. But it is the job of the historian to discern what he can reliably take from this “corrupted history .” He must judge the validity of the descriptions in the same way he judges other primary sources. This volume presents a series of studies by scholars working in Middle Eastern archaeology who actively apply social theory to interpret their fieldwork. It highlights the value of using social theory in the interpretation of fieldwork in a region where, traditionally, such approaches have not played a major role. There are a number of factors that account for why social theory is often under-exploited by archaeologists in this part of the world. In many countries, where large numbers of the foreign archaeologists are involved, a division between those doing fieldwork and those undertaking archaeological interpretation can easily arise. Or, the lack of interest in social theory may stem from a legacy of positivism that overrides other approaches. There is also the fact that archaeology and anthropology often belong to separate academic departments and are considered to be two separate and disconnected disciplines. In some cases, the centrality of historical paradigms has precluded the use of social theory. There are also divisions between universities and other research institutions, such as departments of antiquities, which is not conductive to interdisciplinary cooperation. This factor is especially debilitating in contexts of rapid destruction of sites and the exponential growth of salvage excavations and emergency surveys. The papers presented here integrate a range of perspectives including 'New' or 'Processual' archaeology, Marxist, 'Post-Processual', evolutionist, cognitive, symbolic, and Cyber archaeologies, and touch on many topics including 3D representation, GIS, mapping and social theory, semiotics and linguistics, gender and bioarchaeology, social and technical identities, and modern historical modelling and social practices in Middle Eastern archaeology.

Archaeology and material cultural heritage enjoys a particular status as a form of heritage that, capturing the public imagination, has become the locus for the expression and negotiation of regional, national, and intra-national cultural identities. One important question is: why and how do contemporary people engage with archaeological heritage objects, artefacts, information or knowledge outside the realm of an professional, academically-based archaeology? This question is investigated here from the perspective of theoretical considerations based on Yuri Lotman's semiosphere theory, which helps to describe the connections between the centre and peripheries of professional archaeology as sign structures. The centre may be defined according to prevalent scientific paradigms, while periphery in the space of creolisation in which, through interactions with other culturally more distant sign structures, archaeology-related non-professional communities emerge. Anthropology of the Middle East has implicitly and explicitly been a journal with a regional orientation. Most previous issues, however, have added a thematic dimension to this regional orientation, and the same applies to this special issue. The chosen theme is anthropological archaeology, given the fact that this school in archaeology has been responsible for tremendous progress in Middle Eastern archaeology and has advanced our knowledge of the ancient Middle East by leaps and bounds. Anthropological archaeology has been a major player in Middle Eastern archaeology for the past half-century, and no other school in Middle Eastern archaeology can claim to have been immune from its influence, whether in matters of theory or, more visibly, in methodology. Archaeology of the Middle East (Near East, in archaeological parlance) always has been an enticing field for professional archaeologists and archaeology aficionados alike. Beginning in the mid-nineteenth century and continuing into the early decades of the twentieth century, large-scale and high-profile excavations, predominantly inspired by biblical accounts or imperial competition among European powers, marked the 'Golden Age' of archaeology in the Middle East, when many excavated archaeological sites revealed awe-inspiring palaces of long-forgotten rulers and temples of heathen gods and, in the absence of any meaningful set of antiquities laws, poured invaluable artefacts and hoards of cuneiform tablets into major museums in Europe and the United States. Following World War II, as the new economic conditions in the West hindered such grandiose archaeological adventures, another, more subtle movement in archaeology was about to shift the focus from large-scale excavations aimed, among other things, at discovering lost cities and civilisations to much smaller exposures focused on more humble, but arguably more important, questions pertaining to the early stages of human development. The rise of New Archaeology in the United States and England was changing the theoretical and methodological configuration of archaeology and pushing for a closer intellectual and methodological affiliation with anthropology and other social and natural sciences.

Interestingly, the site appears to have stronger connections with Mesopotamia than with western Iran. These findings shed light on the gradual differentiation of society during the Chalcolithic period, a critical period that witnessed the emergence of the first porto-urban communities in southern Mesopotamia. ## Abstract

![Image 10: sparkles](https://c.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)

In an interview with Donald A. Yerxa, David Wengrow discusses his book on the ancient Near East and its implications for modern understandings of civilization. Wengrow emphasizes the importance of new archaeological findings that reveal sophisticated interconnectedness among early societies, challenging traditional narratives that separate the ancient Near East from the broader historical context. He advocates for a reevaluation of the concept of civilization, stressing the need to recognize the similarities and shared developments between ancient societies and contemporary ones.

This volume presents a series of studies by scholars working in Middle Eastern archaeology who actively apply social theory to interpret their fieldwork. It highlights the value of using social theory in the interpretation of fieldwork in a region where, traditionally, such approaches have not played a major role. There are a number of factors that account for why social theory is often under-exploited by archaeologists in this part of the world. In many countries, where large numbers of the foreign archaeologists are involved, a division between those doing fieldwork and those undertaking archaeological interpretation can easily arise. Or, the lack of interest in social theory may stem from a legacy of positivism that overrides other approaches. There is also the fact that archaeology and anthropology often belong to separate academic departments and are considered to be two separate and disconnected disciplines. In some cases, the centrality of historical paradigms has precluded the use of social theory. There are also divisions between universities and other research institutions, such as departments of antiquities, which is not conductive to interdisciplinary cooperation. This factor is especially debilitating in contexts of rapid destruction of sites and the exponential growth of salvage excavations and emergency surveys. The papers presented here integrate a range of perspectives including 'New' or 'Processual' archaeology, Marxist, 'Post-Processual', evolutionist, cognitive, symbolic, and Cyber archaeologies, and touch on many topics including 3D representation, GIS, mapping and social theory, semiotics and linguistics, gender and bioarchaeology, social and technical identities, and modern historical modelling and social practices in Middle Eastern archaeology.

Archaeology and material cultural heritage enjoys a particular status as a form of heritage that, capturing the public imagination, has become the locus for the expression and negotiation of regional, national, and intra-national cultural identities. One important question is: why and how do contemporary people engage with archaeological heritage objects, artefacts, information or knowledge outside the realm of an professional, academically-based archaeology? This question is investigated here from the perspective of theoretical considerations based on Yuri Lotman's semiosphere theory, which helps to describe the connections between the centre and peripheries of professional archaeology as sign structures. The centre may be defined according to prevalent scientific paradigms, while periphery in the space of creolisation in which, through interactions with other culturally more distant sign structures, archaeology-related non-professional communities emerge. On the basis of these considerations, we use collocation analysis on representative English language corpora to outline the structure of the field of archaeology-related non-professional communities, identify salient creolised peripheral spaces and archaeology-related practices, and develop a framework for further investigation of archaeological knowledge production and reuse in the context of global archaeology.

Apart from wars, other contexts of social conflict have recently become a setting in which archaeologists are faced with acute, sometimes armed, violence. On the African continent, a region often overlooked in discussions of “archaeology in conflict”, rapid economic development has led to several such scenes. The paper discusses a particularly poignant example from the Middle Nile valley in Sudan, where large dam projects have been met with various levels of opposition by affected populations. Local communities opposing the construction of further planned dams on the Nile are increasingly stressing ‘cultural survival’ and fear of ‘developmental genocide’ as two of their major motivations for fighting these projects. Assuming a close link between the developer and archaeological salvage missions, affected people have started to use the expulsion of salvage teams from their territory as a strategy of resistance—posing an ethical dilemma for the archaeologists who struggle to find a position in the increasingly violent controversies accompanying these contested development projects.

The entirety of the written records on the city of Sijilmâsa are cause for frustration: of the more than forty written sources on the city of Sijilmasa that exist today, nearly all are meager, with the exception of the descriptions left by Al-Bakri (late 11th century AD) and Al-Idrisi (second half of the 12th century AD), neither of whom actually visited the city. This relative scarcity of documentation stands in contrast to the significant notoriety of Sijilmasa as one of the principle " ports " and entrepôts of trans-Saharan commerce, where the merchants of the Islamic world would pass several months at a time before undertaking the sixty-day journey across the desert in the direction of the kingdoms of Ghana or Mali. This interesting documentary pattern (the notoriety of the city versus the scarcity of written resources) is illustrative of the paradoxical position of Sijilmasa in the history of the medieval powers and empires of the Maghreb, at once an important center of long-distance trade, and at the same time located on the political periphery, on the edge of the desert in the extreme south of the Maghreb. This tension between center and periphery has always been a source of interest and inspiration in the history of Sijilmasa and for precisely this reason, a study incorporating the historical and archaeological data in an illustration of this dynamic at the site-wide scale would be an essential resource. The book reviewed here was supposed to be just such a work: a long-awaited synthesis of the excavations conducted by the Moroccan-American Project at Sijilmasa (MAPS) under the direction of Ronald A. Messier over the course of six campaigns between 1988 and 1998. The result, however, is disappointing.

## FAQs

![Image 14: sparkles](https://c.academia-assets.com/images/icons/sparkle.svg)
AI

What key findings challenge existing notions of civilization in the ancient Near East?add

Recent research shows extensive cultural exchanges across the Near East long before writing systems existed, altering perspectives on civilization. For instance, material flows like metals and oils reveal interconnectivity across regions such as Turkmenistan and Arabia.

How have archaeological discoveries reshaped the understanding of ancient trade relationships?add

Evidence suggests that trade in everyday items, alongside luxury goods, highlights a complex network in ancient societies. These findings, accumulating continuously, underscore the interconnectedness of regions from the Indus Valley to the Mediterranean.

What implications do new findings have for the concept of civilization?add

The idea of civilization may oversimplify historical connections and shared practices among societies. Wengrow argues that understanding these connections challenges the linear progression narrative often associated with civilization.

How does the interplay of commerce and cosmology manifest in ancient societies?add

Elites in ancient Mesopotamia intertwined commerce with religious beliefs, showcasing how trade was regulated through divine concepts. This relationship echoes modern economic systems, where branding parallels sacred rituals.

Why has the significance of the ancient Near East been overlooked in grand narratives?add

Grand historical accounts often neglect the ancient Near East due to biases towards localized perspectives. Scholars like Daniel Lord Smail emphasize a unified human history, yet fail to recognize important transitional dynamics in these ancient societies.

The paper considers how the traditional focus of Near Eastern Archaeology, which was centred on Mesopotamia and the surrounding areas of Syro-Palestine, Anatolia and Iran, has been challenged, in several ways and for several reasons, by recent developments of the discipline, whose geographical limits have thus become increasingly vague. Examples are given of how recent field activities, by revealing deep and in some cases unsuspected connections with areas which are traditionally the object of different disciplines and have developed a different scholarly tradition, encourage a renewed interest on long-distance circulation and diffusion of raw materials, artefacts and ideas, but at the same time require a deep readjustment of our theoretical frameworks and even of our scientific background. Anthropology of the Middle East has implicitly and explicitly been a journal with a regional orientation. Most previous issues, however, have added a thematic dimension to this regional orientation, and the same applies to this special issue. The chosen theme is anthropological archaeology, given the fact that this school in archaeology has been responsible for tremendous progress in Middle Eastern archaeology and has advanced our knowledge of the ancient Middle East by leaps and bounds. Anthropological archaeology has been a major player in Middle Eastern archaeology for the past half-century, and no other school in Middle Eastern archaeology can claim to have been immune from its influence, whether in matters of theory or, more visibly, in methodology. Archaeology of the Middle East (Near East, in archaeological parlance) always has been an enticing field for professional archaeologists and archaeology aficionados alike. Original discussions on the public role of history and historians from a pantheon of notable experts  
  
Recent Themes on Historians and the Public represents some of the best recent writing on the public role of historians. These articles and interviews from Historically Speaking examine the relationship between historians and their audiences. Award-winning "popular historian" Adam Hochschild begins by discussing the relationship between popular and academic history. An all-star cast of historians and editors offer their responses, forming a fascinating extended conversation. This forum addresses questions such as what the public role of the historian should be and whether practicing history requires a license. In addition the book contains a candid exchange about the state of the history profession at the beginning of the twenty-first century.   
  
Designed to engage both students and general readers, Recent Themes on Historians and the Public illuminates the controversy over the role of historians in the public sphere.

Donald Yerxa was born in Portland, Maine in 1950. From 2001 until 2013, he was a senior editor of Historically Speaking, a journal of historical ideas published by The Johns Hopkins University Press, and from 2011 to 2020, he was editor of Fides et Historia, the peer-reviewed journal of the Conference on Faith and History. He served as an officer of the Historical Society from 2001 to 2014. He is professor of history emeritus at Eastern Nazarene College in Quincy, MA and now resides in Florida.
